## Summary

I reviewed all 10 source files (no `package.json`/lockfile present, so no dependency findings). I found **2 exploitable findings**, both real data-flow issues confirmed by runtime tests rather than pattern matches:

### 1. CRITICAL — SSRF / key-injection via `jku` (`ssrf`)
- `src/oauth/token.js` → `src/oauth/jwks.js`
- `verifyExternalToken` fetches the verification key from `header.jku` (attacker-controlled JWT header). The only guard in `fetchKey` is `String(url).startsWith('https://keys.example.test')` plus `redirect: 'follow'`.
- Verified bypasses: `https://keys.example.test@169.254.169.254/latest/` (userinfo → host `169.254.169.254`) and `https://keys.example.test.evil.com/k` (subdomain → attacker host). Since the fetched text is used as the JWT verification key, an attacker can host their own key and forge any "external" token (authentication bypass) — and the SSRF reaches internal/cloud-metadata hosts.
- The intended safe design exists in `src/http/safe-jwks.js` (fixed URL, `redirect: 'manual'`) but isn't used.

### 2. HIGH — OAuth redirect-URI prefix-match bypass (`open-redirect`)
- `src/oauth/register.js` + `src/oauth/client-repo.js`
- `validateRedirect` uses `redirectUri.startsWith(client.baseUrl)`. Verified that `https://portal.example.test.evil.com/cb` and `https://portal.example.test@evil.com/cb` both pass while resolving to attacker hosts, leaking the authorization code/token.
- A correct exact-match implementation ships in `src/oauth/exact-redirect.js` but is unused.

### Clean (no findings)
`pkce.js` (S256), `state.js` (32-byte random + length-checked `timingSafeEqual`), `config.js` (no secrets), `logging.js` (logs only clientId/outcome), `client-repo.js` (no secret), `safe-jwks.js` (fixed URL, manual redirect).

No audited source files were modified (`source_modified: false`).
